fact: Mark Broadie's analysis of PGA TOUR ShotLink data found tour players one-putt half the time from 8 feet, while amateurs who average a score of 90 one-putt half the time from 5 feet and average two putts from 19 feet, against 33 feet for tour players.
quote: PGA TOUR golfers one-putt 50% of the time from a distance of eight feet. … By contrast, amateur golfers with an average 18-hole score of 90 (90-golfers), one-putt 50% of the time from five feet. … PGA TOUR golfers average two putts from 33 feet, i.e., the fraction of one-putts equals the fraction of three-putts. Amateur 90-golfers average two putts from 19 feet.
source_label: Mark Broadie, Assessing Golfer Performance on the PGA TOUR (Columbia Business School; to appear in Interfaces; version of April 8, 2011)
notes: Read in full with curl and pdftotext on 2026-09-25 (section 3.3, Putting benchmark). The 8-foot result is from 2009 ShotLink data; Figure 3 uses 2003-2010 data. The 90-golfer figures are Broadie's amateur benchmark.

fact: Broadie's putting tables group putts as short (0 to 6 feet), medium (7 to 21 feet) and long (22 feet and over), and he found amateurs who average 90 three-putt about 2.3 times a round, four times as often as tour players.
quote: Table 4: Putting strokes gained per round, broken down into three distance categories: short putts (0-6 feet), medium length putts (7-21 feet) and long putts (22 feet and over). … Amateur 90-golfers three-putt about 2.3 times per round, or four times more often than pros.
source_label: Mark Broadie, Assessing Golfer Performance on the PGA TOUR (Columbia Business School; to appear in Interfaces; version of April 8, 2011)
notes: The bands are Broadie's reporting categories, not a USGA standard; the page uses them to size a green by practice goal.

fact: The Rules of Golf set the hole at 4¼ inches (108 mm) across and at least 4 inches (101.6 mm) deep, with any lining sunk at least 1 inch below the putting green surface unless the soil requires it closer.
quote: The hole must be 4 ¼ inches (108 mm) in diameter and at least 4 inches (101.6 mm) deep. If a lining is used, its outer diameter must not exceed 4 ¼ inches (108 mm). The lining must be sunk at least 1 inch (25.4 mm) below the putting green surface, unless the nature of the soil requires that it be closer to the surface.
source_label: The R&A, Rules of Golf: Definitions (Hole)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25; the definition text sits in the page's embedded JSON (definitionText for 'Hole'). usga.org answers automated fetches with 403, so the R&A's copy of the joint Rules is the source read. The Rules are revised on a four-year cycle; re-read when a new edition takes effect.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says the 3-foot radius around a putting green cup must be flat, smooth and true, checked with a level before the cup goes in, that the putting surface is then laid over the cup and cut around it, and that cups sit ¼ inch below the putting surface.
quote: When the grading and compaction of the sub grade materials are complete, take a level and check the 3’ radius around where the cup is to be placed to make sure it is flat without any imperfections. The 3’ radius around the putting green cup is very important to be flat, smooth and true. … When the putting green cup installation is complete, place the desired putting green surface over the cup and precisely cut the putting green turf around the perimeter of the cup. … Putting green cups should be placed ¼ inch below putting green surface.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Installing Putting Green Cups
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25 (published 2016-07-19, modified 2022-12-29 per the page's schema). A distributor's installer column, not a standard.

fact: The same columnist recommends setting putting green cups in concrete, performance concrete where frost heave is high, and keeping every cup at least 3 feet from the outside fringe.
quote: I highly recommend placing putting green cups in concrete. And for areas that have high frost-heave, please use performance concrete. … And remember, always keep the cups at least 3 feet away from the exterior fringe!
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality (Apr. 30, 2026)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The same article says many greens are 'just for fun' with 'no need to speak about “stimpmeter speeds” and “undulations”', used in one FAQ answer; see backyard-putting-green-size.sgw-just-for-fun.

fact: SGW's installer columnist advises interviewing the client first, because many putting green installations are just for fun and may not need any talk of stimpmeter speeds or undulations.
quote: When you have your first meeting with the client, I recommend doing an interview. Take some time and listen to what their needs are. Find out how experienced they may be. Many putting green installations are just for fun, and there may be no need to speak about “stimpmeter speeds” and “undulations”.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality (Apr. 30, 2026)

fact: SGW's columnist says deep freezing can move the soil and heave the compacted soil around a cup into a 'volcano', that at installations he revisited over two decades cups set in concrete outlasted cups set in dirt, and that a sunk cup can be loosened and lifted back to the proper height.
quote: There may be a downside to placing concrete around cups in extreme freezing temperatures. When the ground freezes during winter months, deep freezing may cause vertical and horizontal movement of the soils, which may cause the compacted soil around the cup to heave into a crown resembling a “volcano.” … I have visited past installations spanning two decades, and cups placed in concrete were still in great condition, including the area around them. … Cups placed in concrete outlasted cups that were placed in dirt by far. … When the cup loosens, spin counterclockwise while slowly lifting to the proper elevation needed.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Are Your Cups Sinking? (Mar. 22, 2022)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. Cup repair itself belongs to the maintenance and repair guides; this page uses it only as a question to ask an installer.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse says a turf putting green can have as many holes as the space allows, that extremely small spaces may be limited to one hole, that cup covers let you rotate which targets are active, and that turf greens can be built to fit narrow side yards.
quote: Turf putting greens are completely customizable and can be designed to fit small, narrow side yards or large, sprawling lawns. … Your outdoor putting green can have as many holes as your space allows! While extremely small spaces may be limited to one hole, the highly customizable nature of synthetic turf putting greens means that you can design your course to have multiple cup locations wherever there’s available space. … You can also use cup covers to rotate active targets and incorporate custom flags and markers to make the space feel like your own private practice facility.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, FAQs Answered: Everything To Know About Installing a Synthetic Turf Putting Green (Aug. 28, 2025)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The same page's line that a green 'can boost home value' is not used.

fact: SGW's installer columnist says putting green fringe can be several feet wide or as narrow as six inches, is needed unless you want balls rolling off the green, helps a green with enough infilled fringe keep its shape, and is best cut in long runs from rolls that are mostly 15 feet wide, split down the middle to about 7 feet 6 inches a side.
quote: Depending on the design, synthetic turf fringe can be several feet in width and as narrow as six inches. Do you need it? Unless you want the ball to roll off of the green, I would say yes. … Did you know that a putting green with a good amount of infilled fringe will keep its shape longer? … I always recommend designing the green so you can maximize long fringe runs. Cut down the center of a full roll of fringe and use the two sections for the left and right sides of the putting green. Most rolls are 15 feet wide, and cutting down the middle will give you approximately 7’6”.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Putting Green Fringe: Which Way Do I Go? (Feb. 15, 2021)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The fact's 'best cut in long runs' paraphrases the columnist's recommendation; the page never uses 'best' in its own voice. Fringe pile height belongs to the pile-height guide; chipping from fringe to the chipping guide.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's spec sheet for its Putting Green PP 40 lists a pile of about 0.50 inches and manufactured rolls 15 feet wide by 100 feet long.
quote: Pile Height: Approx. 0.50 Inches … Manufactured Rolls … Width: 15 Feet Length: 100 Feet
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Putting Green PP 40 spec sheet (PDF)
notes: Read with curl and pdftotext on 2026-09-25 (sheet revision REV082826). One product's roll width; the page says 'can' for a seamless putting surface, not that every green is one piece.

fact: Southwest Greens, a putting green builder, says most backyard putting greens are 300 to 800 square feet and its residential greens are usually around 500, while its commercial greens usually run about 1,500 square feet.
quote: Backyard golf greens for residential spaces are usually around 500 square feet, while artificial golf greens for commercial projects or Nicklaus Design golf courses are usually 1,500 square feet. … Most backyard putting greens are 300-800 square feet, which provide great space for putting, including short “chip shots”.
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The same FAQ quotes per-square-foot prices; never use them (no prices on NoCo pages).

fact: The USGA's Stimpmeter booklet says to measure green speed on a level area about 10 to 12 feet long, ideally a 12-foot level run, or as short as 6 feet using the half-length notch.
quote: Step 1: Select a level area on the green, approximately several feet wide and 10 to 12 feet in one direction. … The ideal method is to measure greens on a 12-foot level area using the standard ball-release notch, or full-length run. … using the “2X” notch on the reverse allows for testing of level areas as short as 6 feet.
source_label: USGA, Stimpmeter Instruction Booklet (archived copy, Apr. 11, 2023)
notes: usga.org answers automated fetches with 403; the PDF was read from the Wayback Machine capture of 2023-04-11 with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. The putting-green-stimp-speed guide owns the method; this page uses only the length of level run it needs.

fact: Firestone requires a buffer of at least 3 feet of permeable surface with living and organic landscape material between the edge of artificial turf and any property line.
quote: A minimum of three (3) foot buffer comprised of permeable surfaces with living and organic landscape material shall be required between the edge of the artificial turf and any property line.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.b.iii (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read through the Municode API (api.municode.com CodesContent, jobId 488870 = Supplement 38, the latest job, productId 18062) on 2026-09-25; banner: 'Codified through Ordinance No. 1072, adopted December 10, 2025.' Section 16.6.4 never mentions putting greens, so whether the turf limits and this buffer reach a green is our reading, hedged on the page with 'ask Firestone Planning'.
